articles.title: Readers Share 6 Genius Ways They Outsmarted the System
articles.content:
发现巧妙的捷径能让生活变得更轻松，这种感觉总是让人相当满足。无论是靠灵机一动还是纯粹的运气，这些小小的胜利往往让人感觉像中了大奖。我们邀请读者分享他们如何巧妙地挑战系统的趣事，结果大家都玩得不亦乐乎。

从夫妻俩如何巧妙地独占一排座位开始，到某人发现几乎可以免费观看亚马逊Prime影视节目，这些故事充满了聪明的漏洞、幸运的意外和令人难以置信的"居然奏效"时刻。有些故事会让你捧腹大笑，有些则会让你恍然大悟——原来我也可以这么做！

以下是读者分享的最有趣、最聪明和最出人意料的捷径。

我和丈夫出行时，通常会订一个靠窗的座位和一个靠过道的座位。大约有半数时间，我们能独享整排座位，因为没人想坐中间。如果有人订了中间座位，他们通常也很乐意换位，让我们坐在一起。甚至有一次，有人因为我们让出窗边座位，还买了饮料送给我们。
——玛格丽特·史密斯，弗吉尼亚州弗朗特罗亚尔

亚马逊Prime视频上很多电影和节目即使对会员也需要租赁费。而购物时，我们可以选择稍后的送货时间以换取数字奖励积分。虽然每次通常只有1美元，但如果经常在亚马逊购物的话，这些积分很快就会累积起来。过去几个月我都没有支付过租赁费。此外，这也让我意识到自己之前多有奢侈，总是选择最快送货，即使不需要。
——帕特里夏·尼克松，新泽西州黑肯塞克

我们的金毛卷毛犬塔克非常依赖我妈妈，只要妈妈不在家，它就不愿下床或社交。上次我爸妈出门时，它甚至拒绝离开妈妈的房间去外面。我尝试了零食、吊着它的绳子、开车库门、甚至用FaceTime和妈妈视频。我们手机上有一个应用程序，可以通知家人到家，塔克知道这个提示音——于是我上网找到这个声音播放，它立刻奔到门口迎接妈妈，我得以把它带出去。我感到有点愧疚，但这招确实管用（两次！），而且对大家都有好处。
——卢克·默里，纽约州马诺维尔

孩子们在长时间排队时总是惹麻烦——爬到护栏上、摸脏东西、侵犯别人隐私——这是他们的天性。为了让我在游乐园排队时安分守己，我会和他们玩猜谜游戏，比如用手机上的Heads Up!应用程序。或者我们会边排队边吃午餐（而不是坐在野餐桌上），这样可以最大化利用时间——当然得有强健的胃才能接受这种方式。
——桑德拉·科雷亚，加利福尼亚州诺科

对于演唱会和体育比赛，我总是买最便宜的票。进场后，我会查看转售网站，看看还有谁在最后一刻卖票，这意味着那些座位可能空着。这样我就能享受到好的座位，否则这些座位就会浪费了。
——霍莉·肖，佐治亚州诺克罗斯

当自动答录系统问我按1选择英语，按2选择西班牙语时，我总是按2，即使我不会说西班牙语。这样通常能让我更快地得到服务。工作人员都会笑笑，然后很乐意帮我解决问题。
——朱迪·布林克曼，内布拉斯加州锡拉丘兹

articles.summary:
There’s something oddly satisfying about finding a clever workaround that makes life a little easier. Whether it’s quick thinking or pure dumb luck, those little wins can make you feel like you’ve hit the jackpot. We asked our readers to share the funniest and most relatable times they managed to outsmart the system, and let’s just say they definitely understood the assignment.

From a couple who somehow scored an entire row to themselves on a flight to someone who realized they could watch Amazon Prime movies and shows for practically free, these stories are packed with clever loopholes, happy accidents and “I can’t believe that actually worked” moments. Some will make you laugh, and others might have you wondering why you never thought of it yourself.

Read on for the funniest, smartest and most unexpectedly brilliant ways our readers managed to beat the system.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more true stories, life hacks, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

You are now free toroam about the row

I try to book a window seat and an aisle seat when my husband and I fly together. About half the time, we get the whole row to ourselves because nobody wants to book the middle seat. But if they do, they’re more than happy to swap so we can sit together. Someone even bought us a drink once for giving them the window seat. —Margaret Smith, Front Royal, Virginia

Credit where credit is due

Lots of shows and movies on Prime Video require a rental fee, even for subscribers. And when you place an Amazon shopping order, you can sometimes select a later delivery date in exchange for a digital reward credit. It’s usually only $1, but it adds up if you routinely shop on Amazon. I ­haven’t paid a rental fee in months. Plus, it made me realize I’d become spoiled, always selecting the fastest delivery whether I needed it or not. —Patricia Nixon, Hackensack, New Jersey

Sad dog, new trick

Our goldendoodle, Tucker, is very attached to my mom and won’t get out of bed or socialize if she’s not home. Last time my parents went away, he wouldn’t even leave her room to go outside. I tried treats, dangling his leash, opening the garage door, a FaceTime with my mom. Our phones have an app that notifies us when a member of the family arrives home, and Tucker knows the sound—so I Googled it and played it. He came running to the door to greet my mom, and I got him outside.I felt bad for tricking him, but it worked (twice!) and was better for everyone. —Luke Murray,Manorville, New York

Outside the lines

Kids get into trouble while waiting in long lines—perching on railings, touching gross stuff, invading personal space—it’s just what they do. To keep mine entertained and orderly while we wait in line for rides at amusement parks, we play guessing games, like the Heads Up! app on my phone. Or we’ll eat lunch as we stand in line (rather than settling at a picnic table) to maximize our time—strong stomachs ­required for that one. —Sandra Correia, Norco, California

Upgrade a cheap seat

For concerts and sporting events, I buy the least expensive tickets available. Once I’m inside the venue, I check resale sites to see who still has tickets listed for sale, which probably means people couldn’t make it at the last second and the seats are empty. I’ve made use of great seats this way that would have otherwise gone to waste. —Holly Shaw,Norcross, Georgia

Press your luck

When an automated answering system asks me to press 1for English and 2 for Spanish, I always press 2, even though I don’t speak the language. It usually gets me through much faster. Representatives laugh it off and are happy to get me the help I need. —Judy Brinkman, Syracuse, Nebraska

We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Post a Photo of Someone Without Asking First?
articles.content:
十年前，博客风靡时，我拥有一个迷人的网络小角落，用照片、趣闻和过多的分享记录我的生活。我通过这种方式认识了许多令人难忘的人，感觉温暖如家，充满归属感——直到一切不再如此。

我遇到了一个狂热的追踪者。他是一名被判有罪的罪犯，向我寄来了数百页令人毛骨悚然的便条，以及我孩子学校的照片。我希望自己能优雅地处理这件事，但事实并非如此。我惊慌失措地在凌晨两点删除所有内容，同时从盒装谷物中狼吞虎咽。警察介入后，我失去了整个愉快的数字纪念册，以及我的网络天真。

从那以后，我每年只发布几张家庭照片，并小心监控网络上关于我的信息。虽然仍在专业领域分享许多内容，但很少发布个人信息，不会具体说明地点，几乎从不提及我的孩子。

最近，我和朋友们去吃饭时，有人掏出手机拍群照。我像往常一样礼貌地请求他们不要发布我的照片，或者如果一定要发，请先将我裁掉。

其中一位每天更新Instagram的朋友感到受伤，指责我限制她的自由。她不情愿地发布了裁掉我的照片，并配文：“未出镜者：那个不想和我们一起出现的朋友（她知道自己是谁）。”这句话让我很难过。这并非事实，我非常喜欢那些朋友。但这也让我思考：不经同意就发布别人的照片是否礼貌？

照片在当时看起来很随意，但实际寿命却出奇地长久。一旦照片上传到网络，它就几乎成了永久的。截图、元数据都存在。那些很少上网却总能看到你不想让他们看到的照片的奇怪叔叔们也存在。

这不是偏执，而是数字现实。卡内基梅隆大学的研究人员证明，通过使用面部识别软件，仅凭街头或约会网站上陌生人（他们从未见过面）的照片，他们就能通过社交媒体反向追踪到这个人的姓名、地址、兴趣，甚至在某些情况下，他们的社会安全号码。而这项研究还是2011年的。

自那以后，技术已经进步了很多。例如，2023年，Clearview AI承认从社交媒体上抓取了超过300亿张图片，用于构建其高度准确的面部识别数据库——这些照片大多是人们认为自己仅在和朋友分享的照片。

你那张无害的晚餐照并不存在于真空中。它存在于一个庞大的、可搜索的、永久的真空中，拥有卓越的面部识别软件。除了监控工业综合体（随意！），还有许多日常原因让人们不想出现在照片中。他们可能正在经历分手。他们可能正在应对健康问题。他们可能在见证保护计划中。他们可能只是每张照片上都有一个疯狂的笑容。所有这些都是合理的，不在你的管辖范围之内。

还有一个方面，也是一个重大的实际问题：我们生活在一个摄影无所不在的世界。当你去参加派对、音乐会，甚至图书馆时，你并没有进入一个禁止拍照的区域——你清楚这一点。

如果每个人都需要获得照片中每个人的许可，社交媒体将无法运转。你需要在每个聚会上填写同意书，在每个生日派对上有公证人，仅发布早餐照片就需要一个法律团队。

我讨厌这个争论最终归结为“每个人都这样做”和“这太麻烦了，无法抗争”——但这就是现实，良好的礼仪需要兼顾善意和实际性。你不能期望自己从未被拍摄过，同时又参与正常生活。（有趣的事实：在公共场所录制他人完全合法。）

与大多数礼仪问题一样，这也取决于具体情况。有趣的群照与不经同意拍摄的照片，其中有人看起来很差，是完全不同的。"（但你看起来很自然！"不是夸奖，如果"自然"意味着"像维多利亚时代刚刚听到坏消息，同时张开嘴巴嚼东西的鬼魂。")

关系也很重要——你20年的最好朋友与工作联系人或新认识的人不同。平台也很重要。Instagram上的私密帖子与TikTok上的公开帖子或——上帝帮帮我们吧——Facebook群组中的帖子（你的整个家族都在其中）有着重大区别。（注意：涉及儿童时，礼仪从灰色地带变为明确界线。如果不是你的孩子，请先询问。停止！）

不经同意就发布别人的照片是否礼貌？这取决于具体情况，但不像"直接发布"派所希望的那样简单。对于在私人账户上发布的、朋友间熟知的、有趣的群照：可能有所让步。对于明显以个人为中心的照片、公开发布的照片，或者涉及任何表达过犹豫的人：请先询问。发送一条"嘿，可以发布这张照片吗？"的信息只需两秒钟。

如果有人请求你删除照片，就直接删除。不要附加条件，不要让人内疚，不要叹息作苦状。照片仍会留在你的相机胶卷中。你对那个晚上的记忆不会改变。而保持或不保持的，是你们之间的友谊。

如果你像我一样，不想被发布照片，请知道你并非难搞或偏执狂，下一步不会是去一间没有电力的小屋。你只是在合理地设定自己的数字足迹边界。这不是反社会行为，而是自我意识的表现。如果我礼貌地请求仍被纳入某人的被动攻击性标题，那么至少我会被裁掉。

有没有一段社会互动让你无法停止思考？请发邮件给我们：advice@tmbi.com，或在Instagram上给Charlotte发消息：@CharlotteHiltonAndersen。

articles.summary:
Ten years ago, at the height of blogging, I had a charming little corner of the internet where I documented my life with photos, anecdotes and way too many overshares. I met so many incredible people that way, and it felt warm and community-y and good—until it wasn’t.

I got a stalker. A real one. He turned out to be a convicted felon who sent me hundreds of pages of creepy notes along with a photo of my children’s school. I’d like to say I handled it with grace and equanimity. I did not. I handled it with a lot of panic-deleting at 2 a.m. while stress-eating cereal directly from the box. Police got involved, and I lost my entire cheerful little digital scrapbook, along with my internet innocence.

Since then, I post maybe a handful of family photos a year and keep a careful eye on what information about me is floating around out there. I still post a lot online about myself professionally. But I rarely post anything personal, don’t post where I am specifically and almost never post about my children.

So, when a group of friends and I went out to dinner recently, and someone whipped out a phone for group shots, I did what I normally do and politely asked them not to post pictures of me—or, if they really wanted to, to please crop me out first.

One friend, who updates her Instagram daily, took it personally and accused me of censoring her. She grudgingly posted the photo with me cropped out, captioning it: “Not pictured: the one friend who doesn’t want to be seen with us (she knows who she is).” That stung. It isn’t true; I love those friends. But it also got me thinking: Is it rude to post a photo of someone without asking first?

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, tech, holiday tips, fun facts, humor and travel all week long.

The case for asking first

Photos feel casual in the moment but have a surprisingly long shelf life. Once an image is online, it’s effectively permanent. Screenshots exist. Metadata exists. Weird uncles who are rarely online but somehow always see the one photo you wished they hadn’t also exist.

That’s not paranoia; it’s digital reality. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University demonstrated that by using facial recognition software on the photo of a ­stranger (someone they’d never met, just spotted on the street or on a dating site), they could work backward through social media to identify that person’s name, location, interests and even, in some cases, their social security number. Starting from nothing but a face. And that study is from 2011.

Since then, the tech has gotten exponentially better. For just one example, in 2023, Clearview AI admitted to scraping over 30 billion images from social media to help build its highly accurate facial recognition ­database—largely from photos people thought they were just sharing with friends.

Your innocent dinner shot doesn’t exist in a vacuum. It exists in a vast, searchable, permanent vacuum with excellent facial recognition software. Beyond the surveillance-industrial complex (casual!), there are plenty of everyday reasons people might not want to be in a photo. They could be going through a breakup. They might be dealing with a health issue. They might be in witness protection. They might just have a deranged-looking smile in every photo ever taken of them. All valid. None of your business to override.

The case for just posting it

Here’s the other side, and it’s a big, practical one: We live in a world where photographing everything has become completely normal. When you go to a party, a concert or even the library, you’re not entering a photograph-free zone—and you know it.

If everyone needed permission from every person in the background of a group shot, social media would grind to a halt. You’d need consent forms at every gathering, a notary at every birthday party and a legal team on retainer just to post a brunch photo.

I hate that the argument boils down to “everyone does it” and “it’s too much of a pain to fight”—but that’s what it is, and it’s good etiquette to consider both kindness and practicality. You cannot expect to never be photographed and still participate in normal life. (Fun fact: Recording people in public places is completely legal.)

The variables

As with most etiquette questions, this one comes down to “It depends.” A fun group photo is very different from a candid shot where someone looks terrible and had no idea the photo was being taken. (“But you look so natural!” is not a compliment if “natural” means “like a Victorian ghost who just got bad news while chewing with her mouth open.”)

The relationship matters too—your best friend of 20 years is different from a work contact or new acquaintance. And the platform matters as well. A private post on Instagram is meaningfully different from a public one on TikTok or—heaven help us all—from a Facebook group your entire extended family is in. (Note: When it comes to kids, the etiquette shifts from gray area to bright line. If it’s not your child, ask. Full stop.)

The verdict

Is it rude to post a photo of someone without asking? It depends, but not as much as the “just post it” crowd would like to believe. For casual, flattering group photos posted to a private account among people you know well: You probably have some leeway. For photos clearly centered on an individual, posted publicly or involving anyone who has expressed any hesitation: Ask first. It takes two seconds to send a “Hey, OK to post this?” text.

And if someone asks you to take a photo down, just do it. No caveats, no guilt trips, no martyred sighing. The photo will still live on your camera roll. Your memory of the evening will be unchanged. And what will also remain—or not, depending on how you handle it—is your friendship.

If you’re the person who, like me, would rather not be posted? Know that you’re not being difficult or a paranoid weirdo whose next stop is a cabin without electricity. You’re exercising a reasonable boundary about your own digital footprint. That isn’t antisocial; it’s just self-aware. And if my asking nicely still ends up as someone’s passive-aggressive caption someday? Well, at least I’ll be cropped out.
